disease_label_per_paper: Successfully managed toxic megacolon due to Clostridium difficile infection in a pheochromocytoma patient complicated by cardiogenic and septic shock
presentation_summary: 55-year-old woman self-administered amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for five days after flu-like symptoms, then developed abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, one episode of diarrhea, chills, fever, and hypertensive crisis.
Initial critical illness included mechanical ventilation, mental status change, tachycardia, pneumonia-like lung consolidation, pheochromocytoma crisis, EF 17%, and mixed cardiogenic/septic shock.
During hospitalization she developed abdominal bloating, nausea, vomiting, and no bowel movement for 72 hours. Stool testing returned positive for C. difficile GDH and toxins A/B.

CT showed stomach, small intestine, and large intestine up to the sigmoid colon markedly dilated with thickened walls, gas/content filling, horizontal air-fluid levels, and suspected paralytic ileus secondary to CDI.

She received high-dose oral vancomycin, rectal vancomycin, IV metronidazole, and rifaximin; surgery was considered but deferred because of high operative risk and no perforation/peritonitis. Bowel motility recovered and stool toxins became negative.
